extracted.intended_audience: the people/citizens of the State of New York (voters considering ratification)
extracted.subtask_description: Hamilton's concluding Federalist Paper arguing that the proposed U.S. Constitution should be ratified: addresses economy and expense, safeguards for republican government/liberty/property, amendment practicability, and civic duties of voters. Written as a public appeal to New York citizens in 1788.

rubrics_metrics.name: Net expense of proposed government
rubrics_metrics.description: The sources of additional expense from the establishment of the proposed Constitution are much fewer than may have been imagined; they are counterbalanced by considerable objects of saving; and while it is questionable on which side the scale will preponderate, it is certain that a government less expensive would be incompetent to the purposes of the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extra costs (support of judges, President, etc.) will not be materially consequential under reasonable plans. Savings arise from reduced sessions of Congress (much business shifted to the President) and greatly shortened sessions of State legislatures because national business will no longer occupy them. Example figures: House maybe a fourth-year session, Senate a third or half; State legislators numbering ~2000 now replaced by ~65 national congressmen doing federal business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer of federal business to the Executive reduces congressional session length
rubrics_metrics.description: A great part of the business which now keeps Congress sitting through the year will be transacted by the President ... Hence it is evident that a portion of the year will suffice for the session of both the Senate and the House of Representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Management of foreign negotiations and many appointments/treaties will devolve on the President (with Senate concurrence), leading to shorter terms for both Houses and fiscal savings; treaties and appointments may give additional business to the Senate only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction in State legislature burden and cost
rubrics_metrics.description: State legislatures have been protracted by having to handle United States business; under the proposed Constitution Congress will do all business of the United States without intervention of State legislatures, so State legislatures will only attend to affairs of their particular States and will not have to sit as long as before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current number of state legislators (~2000) will for federal matters be replaced by a much smaller national body (~65), producing clear savings equivalent to potential additional national expenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union's securities for republican government, liberty, and property
rubrics_metrics.description: The additional securities to republican government, to liberty and to property, to be derived from the adoption of the plan, consist chiefly in the restraints which the preservation of the Union will impose on local factions and insurrections, on the ambition of powerful individuals in single States, diminution of opportunities to foreign intrigue, prevention of extensive military establishments arising from inter-state wars, express guaranty of a republican form of government to each, absolute and universal exclusion of titles of nobility, and precautions against State practices that undermine property and credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements are presented as the primary substantive benefits of the proposed Constitution; each item is a separate protective mechanism (e.g., union restrains factions; exclusion of nobility preserves equality; guaranty prevents individual State subversions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency test for critics (analogy to State constitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many alleged defects of the proposed plan (re-eligibility of the Executive, want of a council, omission of a bill of rights, omission of a provision respecting liberty of the press) exist in the existing State constitution; critics who attack the federal plan for defects they excuse in their State constitution lack consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate objections by checking whether the same criticisms apply equally to the critic's preferred local constitution; insincerity is suggested where critics excuse identical imperfections at the State level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality of adopting an imperfect constitution now versus seeking perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be the extreme of imprudence to prolong the precarious state of our national affairs to pursue a perfect plan; perfection is unattainable from imperfect men and collective compromises are inevitable; better to adopt the present plan and amend than to risk anarchy by refusing an imperfect but workable constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments and experience will improve the system over time; the essay warns against recommencing the constitutional process and risking loss of progress in seven of thirteen States already favorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment practicability: subsequent amendments are easier than prior adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: It will be far more easy to obtain subsequent than previous amendments to the Constitution: an alteration to the proposed plan before adoption would require concurrence of thirteen States; alterations after ratification may be effected by nine States (or practically ten), making later amendment much more feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation includes Article V: Congress 'shall call a convention' on application of two-thirds of State legislatures (currently nine), and ratification requires three-fourths of States; thus subsequent amendments can be proposed singly and adopted without the complex compromises required for an original full constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation of Congress under Article V to call amendment conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: By the fifth article of the plan, the Congress will be obliged 'on the application of the legislatures of two thirds of the States ... to call a convention for proposing amendments,' and the Congress 'shall call a convention.' Nothing in this particular is left to the discretion of that body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This peremptory language removes the argument that national rulers could obstruct desired amendments; it ensures a formal route for amendment proposals when two-thirds of states apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of compromise and accommodation in framing a constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Constitution for the United States must consist of a great variety of particulars to accommodate thirteen distinct States; the compacts must be a compromise of many dissimilar interests and inclinations — perfection cannot spring from such materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect different majorities on different questions; initial formation requires management and compromise among many parties, which multiplies difficulties for an original perfect text but makes single subsequent amendments simpler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic duty of voters: judge by conscience not faction
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man is bound to answer whether the proposed Constitution is fit, according to the best of his conscience and understanding, and to act agreeably to the genuine and sober dictates of his judgment. No partial motive, particular interest, pride of opinion, or temporary passion will justify an improper election of the part he is to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voters should avoid obstinate adherence to party, reflect on the national existence at stake, and consider the majority sanction already given by other states; the essay appeals to moderation and honest judgment rather than partisan fervor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of delaying adoption: risk of anarchy, civil war, or military despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: It is imprudent to hazard anarchy, civil war, a perpetual alienation of the States from each other, and perhaps the military despotism of a victorious demagogue, in the pursuit of a perfect plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adoption in time of peace by voluntary consent is rare and fragile; restarting constitutional efforts risks losing the current momentum and exposing the Union to dangerous individuals who oppose national government in every shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone of political advocacy: avoid personal asperity and calumny
rubrics_metrics.description: The author has addressed himself purely to the judgments and studiously avoided asperities which disgrace political disputants; the charge of conspiracy against the liberties of the people (brought against advocates) is wanton and malignant and provokes indignation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good advocacy concentrates on reasoned argument, not misrepresentation or abusive language; avoid unwarrantable concealments and misrepresentations used to keep truth from the public.
